title: Fish Nutrition
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Fish Nutrition curriculum: macronutrients (protein, lipid, carbohydrate) and their roles, essential amino and fatty acids, vitamins and minerals, energy metabolism and requirements, feed ingredients and formulation, anti-nutritional factors, feed conversion ratio, and feeding practices in fish culture.

questions.question: Fish nutrition is primarily concerned with the study of:
options: The dietary requirements of fish and how nutrients are utilized for growth, maintenance, and reproduction
The behaviour of fish in the wild
questions.correct_answer: The dietary requirements of fish and how nutrients are utilized for growth, maintenance, and reproduction
questions.explanation: Fish nutrition examines the nutrient needs of fish and how diet composition affects growth performance, health, and reproductive success, forming the basis for feed formulation.

questions.question: Compared to most terrestrial livestock, fish generally require a diet with:
options: A higher percentage of dietary protein
A much lower percentage of dietary protein
Only carbohydrates and no other nutrients
questions.correct_answer: A higher percentage of dietary protein
questions.explanation: Fish typically require 25-50% dietary protein depending on species and life stage, considerably higher than the requirement for most terrestrial farm animals, because protein serves as a major energy source as well as for growth.

questions.question: Amino acids that a fish cannot synthesize in sufficient quantity and must obtain from the diet are called:
questions.correct_answer: Essential amino acids
questions.explanation: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized by the fish's body at a rate sufficient to meet its needs and must therefore be supplied through the diet.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the essential amino acids required in fish diets?
questions.correct_answer: Lysine
questions.explanation: Lysine is one of the ten essential amino acids required by fish, and it is often the first limiting amino acid in plant-based fish feed ingredients.

questions.question: The 'limiting amino acid' in a fish feed formulation is defined as:
options: The essential amino acid present in the lowest amount relative to the fish's requirement, constraining protein synthesis
The amino acid present in the largest quantity in the feed
An amino acid that is toxic to fish
questions.correct_answer: The essential amino acid present in the lowest amount relative to the fish's requirement, constraining protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Protein synthesis is limited by whichever essential amino acid is in shortest supply relative to need, similar to the weakest link in a chain, regardless of the abundance of other amino acids.

questions.question: Lipids in fish diets serve primarily as a source of:
options: Concentrated energy and essential fatty acids
questions.correct_answer: Concentrated energy and essential fatty acids
questions.explanation: Dietary lipids provide a highly concentrated energy source (more than double that of protein or carbohydrate per gram) and supply essential fatty acids fish cannot synthesize.

questions.question: Which class of fatty acids is generally considered essential in fish diets, particularly for marine and coldwater species?
questions.correct_answer: Omega-3 (n-3) highly unsaturated fatty acids
questions.explanation: Omega-3 fatty acids, such as EPA and DHA, are essential fatty acids that fish cannot synthesize adequately and must obtain from the diet for normal growth and cell membrane function.

questions.question: 'Essential fatty acid deficiency' in cultured fish commonly manifests as:
options: Poor growth, fin erosion, and reduced reproductive performance
Excessive rapid growth beyond normal rates
No observable effect on the fish
questions.correct_answer: Poor growth, fin erosion, and reduced reproductive performance
questions.explanation: A lack of essential fatty acids in fish diets commonly leads to symptoms such as reduced growth, fin/tail erosion, and poor reproductive outcomes.

questions.question: Carbohydrates in fish diets are generally utilized:
options: Less efficiently than in terrestrial animals, because most fish have limited capacity to digest and metabolize them
More efficiently than protein as an energy source in all fish species
As the sole source of essential fatty acids
questions.correct_answer: Less efficiently than in terrestrial animals, because most fish have limited capacity to digest and metabolize them
questions.explanation: Most fish, especially carnivorous species, have limited amylase activity and glucose tolerance, making carbohydrates a less efficient energy source compared to protein and lipid.

questions.question: Despite their limited digestibility, carbohydrates are still included in fish feed formulations mainly because they:
options: Provide a relatively cheap energy source and act as a binder to improve pellet stability
Are toxic to fish and included as preservatives
Increase the fish's requirement for protein
Have no function in feed at all
questions.correct_answer: Provide a relatively cheap energy source and act as a binder to improve pellet stability
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates such as starch are inexpensive energy sources and also serve as binding agents that help hold feed pellets together during processing and in water.

questions.question: Vitamins in fish nutrition are best described as:
options: Organic compounds required in small amounts for normal metabolic function that the fish cannot synthesize sufficiently
Inorganic elements required in large quantities
The primary source of dietary energy
Structural components of fish bone only
questions.correct_answer: Organic compounds required in small amounts for normal metabolic function that the fish cannot synthesize sufficiently
questions.explanation: Vitamins are organic micronutrients essential for normal physiological processes; fish generally cannot produce them in adequate amounts and require dietary supplementation.

questions.question: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency in cultured fish commonly causes:
options: Scoliosis/lordosis (spinal deformities) and impaired wound healing
questions.correct_answer: Scoliosis/lordosis (spinal deformities) and impaired wound healing
questions.explanation: Most fish cannot synthesize vitamin C, and its deficiency leads to collagen formation problems, resulting in spinal deformities, poor wound healing, and reduced disease resistance.

questions.question: Vitamins are broadly classified into two categories based on solubility:
questions.correct_answer: Fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins
questions.explanation: Vitamins are classified as either fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) or water-soluble (B-complex and C), which affects their absorption, storage, and stability in feed.

questions.question: Minerals required by fish in relatively larger amounts, such as calcium and phosphorus, are classified as:
questions.correct_answer: Macrominerals
questions.explanation: Macrominerals like calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and potassium are required in relatively large quantities for bone formation and physiological function, compared to trace minerals needed in tiny amounts.

questions.question: Unlike most terrestrial animals, many fish can absorb which important macromineral directly from the surrounding water through their gills and skin?
questions.correct_answer: Calcium
questions.explanation: Because fish live in an aquatic environment, they can absorb calcium directly from water via the gills and skin, supplementing dietary intake, unlike land animals that rely solely on diet.

questions.question: Phosphorus deficiency in fish diets commonly leads to:
options: Poor bone mineralization and reduced growth
No effect since phosphorus is non-essential
questions.correct_answer: Poor bone mineralization and reduced growth
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is essential for skeletal development and energy metabolism (as part of ATP); its deficiency impairs bone formation and overall growth performance.

questions.question: The gross energy content of feed ingredients is usually determined using which instrument?
questions.correct_answer: Bomb calorimeter
questions.explanation: A bomb calorimeter measures the total heat released when a feed sample is completely combusted, giving its gross energy value.

questions.question: The feed conversion ratio (FCR) in aquaculture is calculated as:
options: Weight of feed given divided by weight gain of fish
Weight gain of fish divided by weight of feed given
Total number of fish divided by total feed cost
Length of fish divided by weight of feed
questions.correct_answer: Weight of feed given divided by weight gain of fish
questions.explanation: FCR = feed input (kg) / weight gain (kg); a lower FCR indicates more efficient conversion of feed into fish biomass.

questions.question: If 200 kg of feed produces 100 kg of fish weight gain, the feed conversion ratio (FCR) is:
questions.explanation: FCR = feed given / weight gain = 200 kg / 100 kg = 2.0, meaning 2 kg of feed was needed to produce 1 kg of fish weight gain.

questions.question: A fish farmer feeds 450 kg of feed over a culture cycle, and the fish biomass increases from 100 kg to 400 kg. What is the FCR?
questions.explanation: Weight gain = 400 kg - 100 kg = 300 kg. FCR = feed given / weight gain = 450 kg / 300 kg = 1.5.

questions.question: Which of the following is classified as a common plant-based protein source used in fish feed formulation?
questions.correct_answer: Soybean meal
questions.explanation: Soybean meal is a widely used plant protein source in fish feeds due to its relatively high protein content and reasonable amino acid profile, unlike the animal-derived options listed.

questions.question: Fishmeal remains a preferred animal protein ingredient in fish feed formulation mainly because it:
options: Has a well-balanced amino acid profile and high digestibility for most fish species
Is the cheapest ingredient available globally
Is toxic and must be avoided
questions.correct_answer: Has a well-balanced amino acid profile and high digestibility for most fish species
questions.explanation: Fishmeal is valued in aquafeeds for its complete essential amino acid profile, high palatability, and high digestibility, though its cost has driven research into alternative proteins.

questions.question: Anti-nutritional factors in plant-based feed ingredients (e.g. trypsin inhibitors in raw soybean) primarily act by:
options: Interfering with nutrient digestion, absorption, or utilization by the fish
Increasing the nutrient content of the feed
Improving the flavour of the feed for fish
questions.correct_answer: Interfering with nutrient digestion, absorption, or utilization by the fish
questions.explanation: Anti-nutritional factors such as trypsin inhibitors, tannins, and phytic acid reduce nutrient bioavailability by inhibiting digestive enzymes or binding nutrients, thereby lowering feed efficiency.

questions.question: Which processing method is commonly used to reduce anti-nutritional factors such as trypsin inhibitors in raw soybean meal before use in fish feed?
questions.correct_answer: Heat treatment (toasting/cooking)
questions.explanation: Heat treatment denatures heat-labile anti-nutritional compounds like trypsin inhibitors, improving the nutritional value and digestibility of soybean meal.

questions.question: Phytic acid, commonly found in plant-based feed ingredients, is considered anti-nutritional mainly because it:
options: Binds minerals such as phosphorus, zinc, and calcium, reducing their bioavailability to the fish
questions.correct_answer: Binds minerals such as phosphorus, zinc, and calcium, reducing their bioavailability to the fish
questions.explanation: Phytic acid chelates essential minerals, forming complexes that are poorly absorbed by fish, thereby reducing the effective bioavailability of those minerals from the diet.

questions.question: The 'protein-to-energy ratio' in fish feed formulation is important because:
options: An imbalance can cause dietary protein to be used for energy rather than growth, reducing feed efficiency
It has no effect on fish growth or feed cost
Fish never use protein for energy under any circumstances
It only matters for herbivorous fish species
questions.correct_answer: An imbalance can cause dietary protein to be used for energy rather than growth, reducing feed efficiency
questions.explanation: If dietary energy is too low relative to protein, fish will catabolize protein for energy instead of using it for tissue growth, an inefficient and costly use of expensive protein.

questions.question: 'Sparing effect' of dietary lipid and carbohydrate on protein in fish nutrition refers to:
options: Non-protein energy sources reducing the need to use dietary protein for energy, allowing more protein to be used for growth
Protein being used exclusively for energy at all times
Fish requiring no energy sources besides protein
A toxic reaction to excess carbohydrate
questions.correct_answer: Non-protein energy sources reducing the need to use dietary protein for energy, allowing more protein to be used for growth
questions.explanation: Adequate lipid and carbohydrate levels 'spare' protein from being catabolized for energy, allowing dietary protein to be directed toward growth (protein synthesis) instead.

questions.question: The typical crude protein requirement in a commercial grow-out diet for Clarias gariepinus (African catfish) ranges approximately between:
questions.explanation: African catfish, being largely carnivorous, generally requires a grow-out diet with roughly 35-40% crude protein for optimal growth performance.

questions.question: Feeding frequency and feeding rate in fish culture are typically adjusted based on:
options: Fish size/age, water temperature, and species-specific feeding behaviour
The colour of the pond water only
The farmer's personal preference with no biological basis
The number of fishing boats available
questions.correct_answer: Fish size/age, water temperature, and species-specific feeding behaviour
questions.explanation: Feeding rate and frequency should be adjusted to fish size, metabolic rate (influenced by temperature), and natural feeding habits to optimize growth and minimize feed waste.

questions.question: Overfeeding in aquaculture ponds is problematic mainly because uneaten feed:
options: Decomposes and degrades water quality by depleting oxygen and increasing ammonia levels
Has no effect on the pond environment
questions.correct_answer: Decomposes and degrades water quality by depleting oxygen and increasing ammonia levels
questions.explanation: Excess uneaten feed decomposes via bacterial action, consuming dissolved oxygen and releasing ammonia, both of which can stress or kill cultured fish.

questions.question: Extruded (floating) fish feed pellets are generally preferred over sinking pellets mainly because they allow:
options: Farmers to visually monitor feeding activity and adjust feed rates, reducing waste
Fish to absorb nutrients without eating the feed
The complete elimination of any need for protein in the diet
Feed to dissolve instantly without being eaten
questions.correct_answer: Farmers to visually monitor feeding activity and adjust feed rates, reducing waste
questions.explanation: Floating pellets remain visible at the water surface, letting farmers observe feeding behaviour directly and adjust quantities, improving feed management and reducing waste compared to sinking feed.

questions.question: Which nutrient class in fish feed is typically included at a low percentage (often below 10-12%) partly because excessive amounts can impair digestion and nutrient absorption?
questions.correct_answer: Crude fibre
questions.explanation: High dietary fibre is poorly digested by most fish and can reduce nutrient digestibility and feed passage efficiency, so it is kept at low levels, typically under about 10-12%, in formulated fish feeds.
